senses: Having a swooping shape or motion.
ety: From swoop + -y.
examples: The car has a swoopy roofline.
The new version is longer and wider. It has a tighter suspension, dual air bags, available antilock brakes and a swoopier look.
Hand-lettering, swoopy and bold, and the cowboy sign painters who practice it are the subject of “Sign Painters,” published this month by Princeton Architectural Press.

senses: Any transverse bar or piece, such as a bar across a door, or the iron bar or stock which passes through the shank of an anchor.
The top tube of a bicycle frame.
ety: From Middle English crose bar, equivalent to cross- + bar.

senses: The act of deifying; exaltation to divine honors; apotheosis.
Excessive praise.
A deified embodiment.
ety: From Middle English deificacion, from Middle French deifier + -acion or borrowed directly from Latin deificātiō(n), from deific(ā) (“deify”) + -tiō(n) (noun suffix), from de(i) (“god”) + -ficō (“make”). By surface analysis, deif(y) + -ication. * In the Christian, theological sense, influenced by the use of deificātiō(n) as Latin translation of Byzantine Greek θέωσις (théōsis).

senses: That cannot be tested; unverifiable
ety: From un- + testable.

senses: Focused on ecological concerns.
ety: From eco- + centric.
examples: Hay's main concern, in the light of an antigreen backlash, is that homocentric democracy is insufficient for the achievement of the ecocentric goals...

senses: A device that uses diffraction (especially X-ray diffraction) to investigate the structure of matter.
ety: From diffract + -o- + -meter.

senses: A small cup of strong black coffee.
The cup in which this coffee is served.
ety: From French demi-tasse (literally “half cup”), from demi- (“half-”) + tasse (“cup”).

senses: A comprehensive summary of, or treatise on a subject, especially theology or philosophy.
A culmination or archetypal example.
ety: From Latin summa.
examples: The painting is a “summa” of the various trends that intertwined and developed during those crucial years of the early sixteenth century in Florence.
Rockefeller Center is at once a summa of the Art Deco style, and a look ahead to the Internationalist style that dominated after World War II.

senses: A monk of the Eastern Church who is also a priest.
ety: From Byzantine Greek ἱερομόναχος (hieromónakhos), from Ancient Greek ἱερός (hierós) + μοναχός (monakhós).

senses: Highly injurious or destructive to life: deadly.
ety: Middle English, from Latin pestilens, from Latin pestis.

senses: Having a collar (or other encircling demarcation).
ety: From Middle English colered, colleryde; equivalent to collar + -ed.

senses: To grin or smile.
ety: Compared by the EDD to dialectal Swedish gimla (“to move the lips in an unseemly manner, to make a wry face, to move the lips awry”). Compare also North Frisian gēmeli (“to move the lips before laughing”). Nall compares Old English ginian; the hard g in this form needs explanation (its standard English descendant is yawn), though the EDD does record a variant form jimble (/ˈjɪmbəl/).

senses: A person who uses a puppet.
Someone who is manipulative and thus able to get people to do what they want or to make events develop in the way they want in a puppet-like manner.
ety: From puppet + -eer.

senses: To skim along (a surface) like a vessel on the water.
ety: Possibly related with shunt (“to cause to move (suddenly)”). Compare Danish skynde (“to hurry”).

senses: A female red grouse, Lagopus lagopus scotica.
ety: From Middle English morhen, perhaps from Old English *mōrhenn, an alteration of Old English worhenn (compare coordinate masculine term mōrhana, a possible corruption of worhana (“pheasant”)), equivalent to moor + hen.

senses: A chick, a baby chicken
ety: From chick + -ie.

senses: A French noblewoman having a rank equivalent to a viscountess
ety: From French vicomtesse. Doublet of viscountess.

senses: A young maidservant.
ety: From Hindi छोकरी (chokrī).

senses: Having a function or usage similar to an infinitive.
ety: From infinitive + -al.

senses: To append (a text) to a quotation of itself.
To deny the existence or significance of (something obviously real or important).
ety: From Quine, named after the American logician and philosopher Willard Van Orman Quine (1908–2000). Verb etymology 1, verb sense 1 (“to append (a text) to a quotation of itself”) was coined by the American cognitive and computer scientist Douglas Hofstadter (born 1945) in his book Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979; see the quotation), referring to Quine’s study of indirect self-reference and in particular Quine’s paradox, the following statement that produces a paradox: “‘Yields falsehood when preceded by its quotation’ yields falsehood when preceded by its quotation.” Hofstadt

senses: One of the basic musical scales or modes used by classical Hindustani ragas, characterized by seven notes (swaras).
ety: Borrowed from Hindi or Marathi थाट (thāṭ).

senses: Erotic love, sexually expressed or chaste, between a man and an adolescent boy.
ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek παιδεραστία (paiderastía, “love of boys”), from παιδεραστής (paiderastḗs, “pederast”), from παῖς (paîs, “child, son, boy”) + ἐραστής (erastḗs, “lover”), from ἔραμαι (éramai, “to love”).

senses: A Japanese folk art movement focusing on inexpensive hand-made everyday items.
ety: Japanese 民衆的な工芸, “hand-crafted art of ordinary people”.
examples: He studied industrial ceramics at the Tokyo Institute of Technology, inspired by a visit to the Japan Folk Crafts Museum in 1938, where he encountered mingei philosophy, and its objects, for the first time.

senses: Synonym of cuttlefish.
ety: From Middle English cutil, codel, codul, from Old English cudele (“cuttlefish”), a diminutive from Proto-Germanic *kudulǭ, from Proto-Germanic *kuddô + -ulǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *gewt- (“pouch, sack”), from *gew- (“to bend, bow, arch, vault, curve”). Equivalent to cod + -le (diminutive suffix). Compare dialectal German Kudele (“cuttlefish”), Norwegian kaule (“cuttlefish”).

senses: Any of several Nordic breeds of dog such as the Pomeranian or Samoyed.
ety: From German Spitz, from spitz (“pointed”); so called from the tapering shape of its muzzle.

senses: One who, or that which, hogs.
A stocking without a foot, worn by coal miners at work.
ety: From hog + -er.
examples: Against these heroes are the puritans, the hoggers of profit, the shysters, the obfuscators, the do-nothings.

senses: One who resurrects an abandoned idea, practice, etc.; a revivalist.
ety: From resurrection (“the act of rising from the dead and becoming alive again”) + -ist (“forms agents of cause; forms adherents of a belief”), coined alongside resurrection man.
examples: We have no taste for enacting the part of literary resurrectionists.
Bank is a theatrical resurrectionist: His New York-based company... specializes in unearthing and staging ‘neglected but worthy’ works.

senses: A health-care practitioner who specializes in chiropractic.
ety: From Ancient Greek χείρ (kheír, “hand”) + πρᾶξις (prâxis, “action, activity, practice”).

senses: An educated wealthy and elite Filipino during the Spanish colonial period of the Philippines.
ety: Borrowed from Philippine Spanish ilustrado.

senses: A ball bearing.
ety: Phonetic respelling of BB.
examples: Flicking beebees across the visual field of a frog will increase its rate of tongue-flicking, but one should not infer from this experimental result that a function of frog tongue flicking is to catch beebees.

senses: The manner or character of a dogmatist; arrogance or positiveness in stating opinion.
ety: From French dogmatisme, from Ecclesiastical Latin dogmatismus. Derived from Latin dogma (“philosophical tenet”), from Ancient Greek δόγμα (dógma, “opinion, tenet”), from δοκέω (dokéō, “to seem good, think”). Treated in the 17th and 18th century as Greek, with plural dogmata.

senses: A traditional Spanish unit of dry measure, equivalent to about 2.3 L.
ety: From Spanish medio (“half, half-celemin, half-real, etc.”), from Latin medius (“half”), from Proto-Italic *meðjos, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“between”). Doublet of medium, media, and mediate.

senses: A tempo mark directing that a passage is to be played in a restless agitated style.
A passage having this mark.
ety: Borrowed from Italian agitato.

senses: A person who takes a nap.
ety: From nap + -er.

senses: A chain of booksellers.
ety: From Middle English congre, from Old French congre, from Latin conger, from Ancient Greek γόγγρος (góngros), from Proto-Indo-European *geng-, *gong- (“a lump, rounded object”).

senses: Describing any physical property that is affected by temperature.
ety: From thermo- + physical.

senses: Resembling fireworks.
ety: From Latin pyrotechnica, from Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) + τεχνικός (tekhnikós, “skillful, workmanlike”). Analyzable as pyro- + technic.

senses: The science and technology of sound.
ety: From sonic + -s.
examples: Rosie: I keep warning her not to over do her sonic practicing. She'll blow a vocal chord or something. Harlan Band: Yeah, well that's one of the dangers when you're hooked on sonics.

senses: The after song; the part of a lyric or choral ode which follows the strophe and antistrophe.
A kind of lyric poem, invented by Archilochus, in which a longer verse is followed by a shorter one.
ety: From Ancient Greek ἐπῳδός (epōidós); see epi-, ode.

senses: The pod and its contents as a vegetable; the mangetout
A hybrid nanomaterial consisting of spheroidal fullerenes encapsulated within a carbon nanotube.
ety: Synchronically, pea + pod; diachronically, from a Middle English predecessor compound.
